title: Design Redundancy for a Compute Cluster
prompt:
You operate a large GPU compute cluster that runs both long distributed training jobs and low-latency inference services. Hardware fails constantly at this scale: GPUs, hosts, network links, whole racks, even a data hall. Design the redundancy, failover and health-checking strategy so that failures cost little work and capacity targets are still met.

Assume **960 nodes of 8 GPUs (7,680 GPUs)** are needed to serve peak demand, spread across three availability zones.
clarify: Which workloads matter most: synchronous training (one failure stops the whole job), online inference (stateless replicas), or both with different priorities?
What availability and recovery targets apply (inference 99.9%? training: how much lost work is acceptable per failure)?
Which failure domains must we survive: one GPU, one node, one rack or top-of-rack switch, a whole zone?
How much spare capacity is the budget willing to hold idle, and may spares run low-priority jobs?
How do we detect failures: hard crashes only, or also silent degradation such as throttled GPUs, ECC errors or slow links?
Is the cluster one region, or may a region be lost entirely?

reference.requirements:
**Functional**
- Detect failed or degraded GPUs, nodes, links and racks quickly and automatically
- Replace or route around them: reschedule inference replicas, restart training from a checkpoint on healthy nodes
- Hold enough spare capacity (N+1 / N+2) for the chosen failure domains; drain nodes for maintenance without an outage

**Non-functional**
- Inference stays within SLO during a single-rack or single-zone loss
- Training loses at most one checkpoint interval of work per failure
- Failure handling never causes a second failure (no cascading overload or thrash)
- Capacity overhead is justified with numbers
reference.estimation:
- Capacity: 960 nodes × 8 = **7,680 GPUs** needed at peak.
- Zone loss: with 3 zones, each serving 320 nodes, surviving the loss of any one zone at full capacity needs 960 / 2 = 480 per zone = **1,440 nodes**: 50% overhead. Accepting graceful degradation (shed low-priority work) instead needs far less.
- Rack loss: say 4 nodes per rack (power-limited), so 80 racks per zone; being N+2 racks means 8 spare nodes per zone, about **2.5%** overhead for rack-level protection.
- Failure rate (assumption, GPUs only): 5% annualised failure rate × 7,680 = **384 GPU failures/year ≈ 1 per day**; including hosts, NICs, optics and cables, expect several incidents a day.
- A 1,024-GPU job sees 1,024 × 5% / 365 ≈ 0.14 GPU failures/day; with hosts, NICs and optics included, interruptions are roughly daily, so restart cost dominates.
reference.data:
- **topology**: `node → rack → row/pod → zone → region`, plus power feed and switch ids. Every placement decision uses it.
- **node_state**(node_id, state: READY | DEGRADED | CORDONED | DRAINING | FAILED | REPAIR, reason, since, last_heartbeat).
- **gpu_health**(node_id, gpu_idx, ecc_errors, xid_errors, temp, throttle_flags, link_status).
- **pool**(name, min_spare, priority class) and **job**(gang, checkpoint_uri, last_checkpoint_step, state).
- An incident log for repairs and RMAs.
reference.design:
```
 Zone A              Zone B              Zone C        (each: racks on separate power/switches)
 [node agent: heartbeat, DCGM-style GPU metrics, link tests]
        │ health stream
        ▼
 health controller ─▶ node_state ─▶ scheduler (topology-aware, gang)
   (quorum, hysteresis)                │ inference: spread replicas across racks/zones, N+k
                                       │ training: gang on one fabric; hot spares per pod
                                       ▼
                     repair queue ◀── cordon/drain ── checkpoints in replicated object store
```
- Agents report GPU errors, thermals and link counters; a controller consensus (no single-agent verdict) moves nodes between states with hysteresis to avoid flapping.
- Failure domains are first-class: replicas of one service are spread so that no rack holds more than a bounded share; the scheduler reserves spares per pod so a training job can swap a node in minutes.
reference.deepdives:
- **Choosing the redundancy level (N+1 vs N+2 vs zone-level).** Match the spare count to the failure domain you promise to survive and its probability. Single-GPU and single-node failures are frequent, so a small pool of hot spares (about 1–2% of nodes) per pod covers them. Rack or switch loss is rarer but removes 4+ nodes at once, so N+2 racks per zone covers it for 2.5%. A full zone loss costs 50% extra hardware to remain at 100% capacity, which is rarely justified; instead drop to a defined degraded mode: reduce the training pool, move interruptible jobs, keep inference at full strength, and accept higher latency for low tiers. Every spare is idle money, so lend spares to preemptible low-priority jobs.
- **Training failover.** A synchronous job is one big failure domain: any lost GPU halts all of them, so cost = detection time + restart + work since the last checkpoint. Reduce each term: heartbeat plus collective-communication timeouts to detect fast; asynchronous multi-tier checkpoints (local NVMe every few minutes, replicated object store every N minutes) so the lost work is minutes, not hours; a hot-spare node already imaged and burn-in tested; elastic restarts that swap or shrink the gang. Trade-off: checkpoint overhead versus expected lost work; the best interval scales roughly with the square root of (checkpoint cost × mean time between failures).
- **Health checking and graceful degradation.** Hard failures are easy; the dangerous ones are *gray failures*: a GPU with rising ECC errors, a link running at half speed, a thermally throttled card that makes the whole gang slow. Combine passive metrics with active probes (a short matmul and all-reduce benchmark on idle nodes), compare against peers (a straggler detector), and cordon on trend, not just on failure. Avoid cascades by rate-limiting automated cordons (never drain more than a bounded share of a pool at once) and failing safe if health data is stale. For inference, use outlier ejection, retry budgets and priority-based load shedding.
reference.wrapup:
- Topology-aware placement, hot spares sized per failure domain (about 2.5% for rack-level N+2; 50% would be needed for a full zone), checkpoint-based training recovery, and active plus passive health checks with controlled automation.
- Trade-offs: idle spare cost vs risk; checkpoint overhead vs lost work; aggressive cordoning vs false positives.
- Next: automated repair and RMA flows, burn-in for new hardware, multi-region disaster recovery.

rubric.text: Defines failure domains (GPU, node, rack/switch/power, zone, region) and which are survived
Sizes spare capacity with arithmetic (N+1/N+2, zone loss needs 50% extra for 3 zones) and justifies the choice
Spreads replicas and jobs across domains with topology-aware placement and limits per-rack concentration
Distinguishes inference (stateless replicas, reschedule) from training (synchronous gang, restart from checkpoint)
Reduces training failure cost: fast detection, multi-tier checkpoints, hot spares, checkpoint interval trade-off
Detects failures with heartbeats and GPU metrics (ECC, thermals, link errors) reported to a replicated controller
Handles gray failures and stragglers with active probes, peer comparison and trend-based cordoning
Avoids cascading failure and flapping: hysteresis, rate-limited automated draining, fail-safe on stale data
Defines graceful degradation: priority classes, preempting low-priority work, load shedding, reduced mode
Covers maintenance and repair lifecycle: drain, cordon, repair queue, burn-in before returning to service
Mentions using spare capacity productively (preemptible jobs) and regional disaster recovery
